Computed

Learning by comparing

Show a network two crops of the same photo and ask it to pick out the partner among many other photos. Nobody labels anything, yet to win this game the network has to learn what makes an image itself. This page builds contrastive learning from that one game: the loss, the tricks that made it work at scale, what it really optimizes, how it fails, and where it lives on today.

Act IThe idea

Learning by comparing

Suppose you have a million photos and no labels at all. Can a network still learn something useful from them? This chapter answers yes, and shows the one trap you must avoid on the way.

The game: two views of one photo

Take one photo of a mug. Crop it in two different places and change the colors a little. You now have two views. They look different pixel by pixel, but they show the same mug. Now take a photo of a bicycle. Its views share nothing with the mug's views.

Here is the game you give the network: put the two views of one photo close together, and keep views of different photos apart. No one has to label anything, because you made the pairs yourself. To play well, the network must ignore what you changed (the crop, the colors) and keep what you did not change (the mug). That is exactly what we want a good feature to do.

A few words you will see on every page from here on. The network that turns an image into a vector is the encoder. Its output vector is the embedding. Two views of the same photo form a positive pair. Views of different photos form negative pairs.

First attempt: only pull

The simplest loss you could write is "the distance between the two views of each photo". Minimize it, and the views of each photo pull together. The figure below trains a small encoder this way. Eight made-up photos each have two views; each blue dot is one view, its yellow ring is the other, and a green line joins them.

Make a guess before you press "Pull only". What is the cheapest way for the encoder to make every pair close?

Press it and watch. Every point slides into the middle. The encoder found a trick: if it sends every image to the same point, every pair has distance zero and the loss is perfect. But now a mug and a bicycle get the same embedding, so the encoder has learned nothing. This failure is called collapse.

Think of a student who answers "same" to every question "are these two the same?". The student is never wrong on the positive pairs, and is useless.

Keep this picture in mind. Every method on this page is, at heart, a way to stop collapse.

The fix: also push

The student cheats because we never ask about different photos. So ask. For every negative pair, add a cost that pushes the two views apart. Give each point a personal-space bubble of radius mmm, called the margin: a negative pair inside the bubble pays a cost, and a negative pair outside it pays nothing.

Now press "Pull and push". Collapse has become the most expensive answer, because when everything sits on one point, every negative pair is deep inside the bubble. The cheapest answer is now the one we wanted: partners close, different photos apart.

The same idea as an equation

Here is the whole loss for one pair of inputs. Read it as "if the pair is positive, pay for distance; if it is negative, pay for closeness inside the margin".

L=(1−Y) 12 DW2+Y 12 {max⁡(0,  m−DW)}2L = \htmlData{step=1, link=pull}{(1-Y)\,\tfrac12\,\htmlClass{t-green}{D_W^2}} + \htmlData{step=2, link=push}{Y\,\tfrac12\,\htmlClass{t-red}{\{\max(0,\; \htmlData{step=3, link=margin}{m} - \htmlData{step=4, link=dist}{D_W})\}^2}}L=(1−Y)21​DW2​+Y21​{max(0,m−DW​)}2

Eq. 4 in Hadsell, Chopra and LeCun, "Dimensionality reduction by learning an invariant mapping", CVPR 2006 (written there as L(W,Y,X⃗1,X⃗2)L(W, Y, \vec X_1, \vec X_2)L(W,Y,X1​,X2​)).

  • DWD_WDW​: the distance between the two outputs of the encoder with weights WWW, one output per input of the pair.
  • YYY: 0 if the pair is similar (two views of one image), 1 if it is dissimilar (views of different images). Only one of the two terms is active for any pair.
  • DW2\htmlClass{t-green}{D_W^2}DW2​: the pull. It is zero only when partners coincide.
  • max⁡(0,m−DW)2\htmlClass{t-red}{\max(0, m - D_W)^2}max(0,m−DW​)2: the push. It is zero once a dissimilar pair is at least mmm apart, so far-away pairs cost nothing and only near ones are pushed.

Try it with numbers. Say the margin is m=1m = 1m=1.

  • A positive pair at distance 0.3 pays 12⋅0.32=0.045\tfrac12 \cdot 0.3^2 = 0.04521​⋅0.32=0.045. It still wants to get closer.
  • A negative pair at distance 0.3 pays 12(1−0.3)2=0.245\tfrac12 (1 - 0.3)^2 = 0.24521​(1−0.3)2=0.245. It is inside the bubble, so it gets pushed.
  • A negative pair at distance 1.5 pays 000. It is already far enough, so the loss leaves it alone.

That last line matters more than it looks. The push only spends effort on negatives that are close. Far-away negatives teach nothing. You will meet this idea again in chapter 7, on hard negatives.

Inside the siamese network: forward, then backward

The loss needs two outputs, one per input of the pair. The network that makes them is called siamese: two copies of one encoder that share every weight. Step through one training pair from the figure above. Make a guess before you press "5 Gradients": there are two encoder copies, so how many sets of weights does one step update?

The answer to the guess: one. The two copies are the same weights, so their gradients add up into a single update. This is why the method is called siamese, after twins who share one body.

Check yourself: what would happen if you trained with the push term only?

Different photos would spread apart, but nothing would pull the two views of one photo together. The encoder would have no reason to ignore the crop and the colors, so two views of the same mug could land far apart. You need both forces: the pull teaches what to ignore, and the push stops collapse.

Where this came from

This loss is from Hadsell, Chopra and LeCun (CVPR 2006), who call it the contrastive loss, the name the whole field now carries. A year earlier, Chopra, Hadsell and LeCun had trained a siamese network for face verification. It is two copies of one network with shared weights, one per input, scored on the distance between their outputs. FaceNet (1503.03832) later used a triplet of anchor, positive and negative, and asked the positive to be closer than the negative by a margin.

Where we go next: from a margin to a lineup

The margin loss has two weak spots. It looks at one pair at a time, so each step sees very few negatives. And you must pick the margin mmm by hand, in units of distance.

Now picture a police lineup instead. Show the network one view (the anchor) and a row of candidates: its true partner and many strangers. Ask it to point at the partner. One question now checks many negatives at once, and "most similar of all" needs no distance scale: a softmax over the candidates measures it.

Sohn's N-pair loss (NeurIPS 2016) made exactly this change for faces and products, using class labels to form the pairs. Later work showed that N-pair is the same loss as InfoNCE, which chapter 3 builds, up to constants, when both inputs go through one encoder and the score is a dot product (Tschannen et al., 1907.13625, Sec. 4). The figure at the top of the page already plays the lineup game, and chapter 3 builds it step by step.

You should now be able to explain

  • Why two augmented views of one photo give a training signal with no labels.
  • Why pulling partners together on its own makes the encoder collapse.
  • How a push with a margin makes collapse expensive, and why far-away negatives cost nothing.

In practice

Comparison is the only signal in self-supervised pretraining, so something must always stop collapse. On this page that something is negatives (Acts I to III), a balancing constraint (chapter 8), labels (chapter 9), or a caption (chapter 10). If a contrastive model you train gives almost the same embedding for very different inputs, suspect collapse first.

The field at a glance

How big is this field, and which branches does this page follow? This chapter gives you a map: a count of papers by year, and a family tree you can come back to.

Optional on a first read: skip to chapter 3 for the mechanics.

Counting papers

One cheap way to see a field is to count how often its name appears. The chart below asks the arXiv preprint server two questions for each year. First, how many papers have the word "contrastive" in the title? Second, how many have the phrase "contrastive learning" in the abstract, the summary paragraph at the top of a paper?

Why 2020 is the turning point

Look at the solid bars first. The phrase "contrastive learning" was almost absent from abstracts before 2020: 17 papers in 2019. Then it jumped to 241 in 2020 and 690 in 2021.

Two papers sit right at the jump. MoCo (first posted 2019-11-13) and SimCLR (2020-02-13) turned the idea of chapter 1 into a recipe that anyone could copy: two augmented views, a standard network, and many negatives. Chapters 4 and 5 open each recipe up. Once a recipe is simple and works, other people start to use it, and the counts follow.

A word becomes a tool

Now compare the two bar colors. Before 2022, more papers put "contrastive" in the title than put "contrastive learning" in the abstract. From 2022 on it is the other way round: 1203 abstracts against 1197 titles that year, and the gap grows through 2025.

Here is our reading of that. A title names what a paper is about. An abstract also names what a paper uses. When the abstract count overtakes the title count, more papers use contrastive learning as one part of a larger method than study it for its own sake. The idea has become a tool.

A warning about the early title bars: "contrastive" is an ordinary English word. In 2019, 183 titles contained it, but only 17 abstracts said "contrastive learning". Many of those early titles are likely about other things, such as contrastive explanations or the contrastive study of languages. The abstract phrase is the cleaner signal.

Where the word spread

The method was born in vision. You might expect images to dominate the counts. Make a guess before you press "image or visual": what share of all "contrastive" titles also name images, and did that share rise or fall after 2020?

Press it. The image count keeps rising: 49 titles in 2019, 240 in 2025. But the dashed share line falls from about a quarter to under a fifth and then stays flat. Now press "text", "graph" and "recommendation". Each of them starts near zero before 2020 and climbs after. The image count grew; the rest of the field grew faster.

That is why a raw count can mislead you. To compare one slice across years, divide it by the whole.

s(y)=nslice(y)nall(y)\htmlData{step=3, link=share}{s(y)} = \frac{\htmlData{step=1, link=slice}{n_{\text{slice}}(y)}}{\htmlData{step=2, link=all}{n_{\text{all}}(y)}}s(y)=nall​(y)nslice​(y)​

Derived here, in our notation: a plain share, not an equation from a paper.

  • yyy: the year of first submission to arXiv.
  • nslice(y)n_{\text{slice}}(y)nslice​(y): the titles that contain "contrastive" and also a topic word, such as image or graph (the solid bars in the topic view).
  • nall(y)n_{\text{all}}(y)nall​(y): all titles that contain "contrastive" (the grey bars).
  • s(y)s(y)s(y): the slice's share of the whole, between 0 and 1 (the dashed line).

Try it with the image slice:

  • In 2019, 49 of 183 titles named images, so s=49/183≈0.27s = 49 / 183 \approx 0.27s=49/183≈0.27: about 27%.
  • In 2021, 142 of 853, so s≈0.17s \approx 0.17s≈0.17: about 17%.
  • In 2025, 240 of 1324, so s≈0.18s \approx 0.18s≈0.18: about 18%.

So the image slice is a steady minority, near a fifth of the titles, while the word spread to text, graphs, recommendation and medicine. This page stays with images, because that is where the ideas were found and tested.

The family tree

Counts tell you how much. The tree tells you who built on whom. Each pill is one paper, placed in a lane: the problem it works on. Time runs down the page. Inside a lane the order is exact; across lanes, papers on the same band share only the year. Solid pills are taught in depth on this page, and dashed pills are named in passing. Press any pill.

Do not worry about the names yet; each solid pill gets a chapter. Come back to this map after chapter 8.

How to read the lanes

Each lane is a question the field had to answer, and each one gets a chapter:

  • Negatives: how do you get many negatives cheaply? Memory bank, CPC, MoCo, SimCLR. This lane is the spine of chapters 3 to 5.
  • Theory: what does the loss actually optimize? Mutual information first, then alignment and uniformity on the sphere (chapter 6).
  • Hard negatives: which negatives teach the most, and which are secretly positives (chapter 7)?
  • No negatives: can you stop collapse without negatives at all (chapter 8)?
  • Labels and Language: what changes when the positive is a same-class image (chapter 9) or a caption (chapter 10)?
  • Dense: can you contrast regions or pixels instead of whole images, for detection and segmentation? This page does not teach it; the guide and chapter 10 point to it.

Now read the bottom half of the tree. After 2021 the image-only lanes add self-distillation papers (DINOv2, DINOv3, Web-SSL), which use no negatives. The lane with new contrastive work is Language: SigLIP, MetaCLIP, SigLIP 2 and Perception Encoder. Our reading: image-only contrastive pretraining peaked around 2020 and 2021, and the image-text form is the one that lives on. The idea of pulling the pair and pushing the rest did not go away; it moved to pairs of images and captions.

You should now be able to explain

  • Why 2020 is the turning point, and which two recipes made the idea easy to copy.
  • Why a slice's share, not its raw count, shows whether it is growing relative to the field, and what a word count cannot see.
  • Which lane of the family tree each later chapter follows, and why the image-text lane is the one still active.

In practice

If you need an image encoder today, you will usually start from a pretrained one, not train your own. In our reading, most such encoders come from two lanes of the tree: Language (CLIP, SigLIP and their successors) and No negatives (DINOv2, DINOv3). The Negatives lane is where the ideas behind both were worked out, which is why the rest of this page starts there. When you search for prior work in your own domain, search for the mechanism as well as the word: many papers that use it never say "contrastive".

InfoNCE: find your partner in a lineup

Chapter 1 ended with a police lineup: show the network one view of a photo and a row of candidates, and ask it to point at the true partner. This chapter turns that game into a loss called InfoNCE, shows what temperature does to it, and explains what the loss measures and what it cannot.

The game: one anchor, N candidates

Take one photo and make two views of it, as in chapter 1. Call one view the anchor. The other view is its partner, also called the positive. Now add views of other photos. These are the negatives. The partner and the negatives together are the candidates, and there are NNN of them: one partner and N−1N-1N−1 negatives.

The encoder turns every view into an embedding. To compare two embeddings we use the cosine similarity: the dot product of the two vectors after each is scaled to length 1. It is 1 when they point the same way, 0 when they are at right angles, and -1 when they point in opposite directions. In the figure, each candidate's similarity to the anchor is the first bar under its card.

First attempt: turn the scores into a choice

A good encoder gives the partner the highest score. But "highest" is not a loss yet. We want one number that is small when the partner clearly wins and large when it does not.

You already know a tool for this: the softmax you use for classification. Exponentiate each score, then divide by the sum, and you get NNN probabilities that add up to 1. The second row of bars shows them. The loss is minus the log of the partner's probability. That is ordinary cross-entropy. The only new thing is what the classes are: not "cat" or "dog", but the NNN candidates in this lineup, with the partner as the correct answer. Every batch brings a new lineup, so there is no fixed list of classes.

This also fixes collapse. If the encoder sent every photo to one point, every candidate would score the same, each would get probability 1/N1/N1/N, and the loss would be log⁡N\log NlogN. That is the loss of a blind guess, the worst a sensible model can do. The only way down is to score the partner above the strangers.

Make a guess before you press "Hard (close)". The negatives become views of other mugs, so they score almost as high as the partner. Will the loss go up or down, and how close will it get to the dashed log⁡N\log NlogN line?

Press it. From the starting state, the partner's probability falls from 0.400.400.40 to 0.290.290.29 and the loss rises from 0.900.900.90 to 1.241.241.24, close to log⁡4≈1.39\log 4 \approx 1.39log4≈1.39. The encoder has not changed; the lineup got harder. You might expect hard negatives to be bad news. In fact they are the useful ones: a negative that already scores far below the partner barely moves the probabilities, so it gives almost no gradient. Chapter 7 returns to this.

The same idea as an equation

Here is the loss for one anchor embedding uuu, with cosine similarity as the score and a temperature τ\tauτ (our notation). Read it as "minus the log of the partner's softmax probability".

L=−log⁡exp⁡(sim(u,v+)/τ)∑j=1Nexp⁡(sim(u,vj)/τ)\htmlData{step=1, link=loss}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathcal{L}}} = -\log \frac{\exp\big(\htmlData{step=2, link=partner}{\htmlClass{t-yellow}{\mathrm{sim}(u, v^{+})}} / \htmlData{step=4, link=temp}{\tau}\big)}{\htmlData{step=3, link=lineup}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp\big(\mathrm{sim}(u, v_j) / \tau\big)}}L=−log∑j=1N​exp(sim(u,vj​)/τ)exp(sim(u,v+)/τ)​

Our notation for InfoNCE (CPC, arXiv 1807.03748v2, Eq. 4), with the cosine score and temperature of Wu et al. 2018 and SimCLR (chapter 5).

  • u\htmlClass{t-blue}{u}u: the anchor's embedding. v1,…,vNv_1, \dots, v_Nv1​,…,vN​: the candidates' embeddings; v+\htmlClass{t-yellow}{v^{+}}v+ is the partner, one of them.
  • sim(u,v)=uTv/(∥u∥∥v∥)\mathrm{sim}(u, v) = u^T v / (\lVert u \rVert \lVert v \rVert)sim(u,v)=uTv/(∥u∥∥v∥): the cosine similarity, between -1 and 1.
  • τ\tauτ: the temperature, a positive number that divides every score before the softmax. The next step explains it.

Try it with the figure's starting numbers. Four candidates, τ=1\tau = 1τ=1, and similarities 0.80.80.8 for the partner and 0.3,0.1,−0.20.3, 0.1, -0.20.3,0.1,−0.2 for the negatives.

  • Exponentiate: e0.8=2.23,  e0.3=1.35,  e0.1=1.11,  e−0.2=0.82e^{0.8} = 2.23,\; e^{0.3} = 1.35,\; e^{0.1} = 1.11,\; e^{-0.2} = 0.82e0.8=2.23,e0.3=1.35,e0.1=1.11,e−0.2=0.82. The sum is 5.505.505.50.
  • The partner's probability: 2.23/5.50=0.402.23 / 5.50 = 0.402.23/5.50=0.40. The negatives get 0.25,0.20,0.150.25, 0.20, 0.150.25,0.20,0.15.
  • The loss: −log⁡0.40=0.90-\log 0.40 = 0.90−log0.40=0.90. A blind guess would cost log⁡4=1.39\log 4 = 1.39log4=1.39.

Notation on this page

NNN here is the number of candidates in one lineup: one partner and N−1N-1N−1 negatives. Later chapters follow their papers and use NNN for the number of photos in a batch; chapter 5 says so where it switches. τ\tauτ always means the temperature.

Temperature: how sharp is the pick?

Look at that example again. The partner wins clearly on similarity, yet it gets only 40%40\%40% of the probability. The reason is that cosine similarity lives between -1 and 1, so the exponentials can differ by a factor of at most e2≈7.4e^2 \approx 7.4e2≈7.4. Even a perfect encoder, with the partner at 1 and three negatives at -1, would get only 1/(1+3e−2)=0.711/(1 + 3e^{-2}) = 0.711/(1+3e−2)=0.71. With 63 negatives that drops to 0.100.100.10.

The temperature fixes this. Divide every similarity by τ\tauτ before the softmax. A small τ\tauτ stretches the gaps between scores, so the softmax becomes sharp. Try τ=0.1\tau = 0.1τ=0.1 on the same four numbers: the scores become 8,3,1,−28, 3, 1, -28,3,1,−2, the partner gets 0.990.990.99, and the loss drops to 0.0080.0080.008. Drag the τ\tauτ slider in the figure and watch the probability bars go from flat to peaked.

You might think the smallest τ\tauτ is always best. It is not. When τ\tauτ is tiny, the softmax looks almost only at the highest-scoring negative, so nearly all the push lands on the negatives that score closest to the partner. Set the figure to hard negatives, N=64N = 64N=64 and τ=0.05\tau = 0.05τ=0.05. Now the probability the partner loses goes almost all to the closest negatives. The rest get almost nothing. Chapter 6 shows what this does to the shape of the embedding.

CPC itself has no temperature. Its score zTWkcz^T W_k czTWk​c is not normalized, so the network can make scores as large as it needs. The temperature comes with unit-length embeddings: Wu et al. (2018) used τ=\tau =τ= 0.07, and SimCLR (chapter 5) made it a standard knob.

What the loss measures: a bound on shared information

CPC gives the loss a second meaning. Its symbols ctc_tct​ (the anchor) and xt+kx_{t+k}xt+k​ (the partner) are drawn in "Inside CPC" below. The mutual information III between two views is how much knowing one tells you about the other, here measured in nats (natural-log units). If the network can pick the partner out of a lineup, the views must share information. CPC turns this into an inequality:

I(xt+k,ct)≥log⁡(N)−LN\htmlData{step=1, link=bound}{\htmlClass{t-green}{I(x_{t+k}, c_t)}} \geq \htmlData{step=2, link=ceiling}{\log(N)} - \htmlData{step=3, link=loss}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathcal{L_{\text{N}}}}}I(xt+k​,ct​)≥log(N)−LN​

CPC (arXiv 1807.03748v2), Sec. 2.3: the unnumbered display just after Eq. 5. It is derived in App. A.1 through a step that is an approximation (Eq. 8). Poole et al. prove the bound without that approximation (Eq. 10, arXiv 1905.06922v1, Sec. 2.3).

  • I(xt+k,ct)\htmlClass{t-green}{I(x_{t+k}, c_t)}I(xt+k​,ct​): the mutual information between the context and the true future piece. Nobody can compute it directly, so we estimate it from below: the bound is a floor under it.
  • log⁡(N)\log(N)log(N): the loss of a blind guess among NNN candidates, the dashed line in the figure.
  • LN\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathcal{L}_{\text{N}}}LN​: the InfoNCE loss. Every nat you take off it raises the floor by one nat.

Read it as "how much better than a blind guess". In the worked example, log⁡4−0.90=0.48\log 4 - 0.90 = 0.48log4−0.90=0.48 nats: the two views share at least that much. The green bracket in the figure is this number.

Now the catch. The loss can never go below 0, so the bound can never go above log⁡N\log NlogN (derived here; Poole et al. state the same cap). Pick the partner perfectly out of 4 candidates, and you have shown only log⁡4=1.39\log 4 = 1.39log4=1.39 nats, even if the two views share far more. In the lineup picture: one correct pick out of four people is evidence, but it cannot prove more than "one of four". CPC notes that the bound "becomes tighter as N becomes larger". Its ceiling is log N, which is one reason contrastive methods want many negatives. Press "Easy (far)", set τ\tauτ small, and watch the loss hit 0 while the bracket stops at the dashed line.

Check yourself: you train with 256 candidates per lineup and the loss sits at 5.555.555.55 for hours. What is the model doing?

Nothing useful. log⁡256=5.55\log 256 = 5.55log256=5.55, so the loss equals that of a blind guess: every candidate gets about the same probability. The bound log⁡N−L\log N - \mathcal{L}logN−L is 0. Suspect collapse, a bug that feeds the wrong partner, or a learning rate that is too high.

A caveat: more information is not the point

The bound makes a tidy story: InfoNCE works because it maximizes mutual information. Tschannen et al. (1907.13625) tested that story and found it incomplete. Mutual information does not change under any invertible transformation of the features. An encoder that scrambles its features in a reversible way keeps all the information, yet a linear classifier on top may find them useless. So information alone cannot explain why the features are good. In their words, maximizing tighter bounds on mutual information "can result in worse representations". Success depends strongly on the encoder architecture. It also depends on how the score function, called the critic, is built.

How do you score an encoder that never saw a label? Freeze it, train one linear layer on top with the labels, and report how often its top guess is right (top-1 accuracy). This is a linear probe; every accuracy on this page uses it unless it says otherwise.

Claim card: Tschannen et al., "On mutual information maximization for representation learning" (ICLR 2020)

Claim
The success of InfoNCE-style methods "cannot be attributed to the properties of MI alone"; it depends on the inductive bias of the encoder and of the critic. A tighter bound can give worse features.
Setup
MNIST digits cut in two: the top half is one view, the bottom half the other. Quality is the linear-probe test accuracy on the top-half features, with batch 128, averaged over 20 runs. Reference points: a linear classifier on raw pixels reaches about 85%, a supervised network about 94%.
Test 1: invertible encoders
An invertible encoder (one whose input can always be rebuilt from its output) keeps all the information, so the true mutual information cannot change. Yet the estimated bound and the linear accuracy both rise during training. An invertible encoder trained adversarially (no MI estimator) ends up worse than raw pixels, although its true mutual information stays at the maximum.
Test 2: critics
Three score functions on the same encoders: a simple bilinear one (xTWyx^T W yxTWy) and two small networks. Measured with the NWJ bound (another estimate of mutual information), the MLP critic is tightest but barely beats raw pixels; the bilinear critic is loosest and gives the best features.
Test 3: same bound, different features
An MLP and a ConvNet encoder are trained to hold the bound at a target ttt of 2 or 4. After 7k iterations both hit the target, but the ConvNet gives clearly higher linear accuracy. Same bound, different features.
Result
Mostly shown in plots, not tables. With batch 128 the InfoNCE estimate is capped at log⁡128≈\log 128 \approxlog128≈ 4.85 nats, and it ends near that cap for every critic, so InfoNCE alone cannot rank them.
What would falsify it
Our reading: a tighter bound that always gave better accuracy across critics, or two encoders at the same bound with the same accuracy.
Scope
Small networks on MNIST halves (CIFAR-10 in the appendix), linear evaluation only. Not tested at ImageNet scale.

The same paper gives a more practical reading of InfoNCE (Sec. 4). Take one encoder for both inputs, and score a pair by the dot product of its two embeddings. Then InfoNCE is the N-pair metric-learning loss from chapter 1, up to constants. Think of InfoNCE as a ranking loss on embeddings, and of the bound as a side fact, not the reason it works.

Inside CPC: forward, then backward

Here is how CPC plays the lineup game on images. It cuts each image into a grid of overlapping patches, encodes every patch, and reads the grid from the top down. From the rows it has seen, it predicts the embeddings of patches up to five rows below. Each prediction is an anchor; the true patch below is its partner.

Make a guess before you press "7 Gradients". Which boxes will the gradient reach, and is anything frozen?

Step 6 is the lineup loss of this chapter. This is the same loss, written in CPC's own notation: the anchor is the context ctc_tct​, and the partner is the patch xt+kx_{t+k}xt+k​ that lies kkk rows below.

LN=−EX[log⁡fk(xt+k,ct)∑xj∈Xfk(xj,ct)]\htmlData{step=1, link=loss}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathcal{L_{\text{N}}}}} = - \mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}_{X}\left[\log \frac{\htmlData{step=2, link=partner}{\htmlClass{t-yellow}{f_k(x_{t+k}, c_{t})}}}{\htmlData{step=3, link=lineup}{\sum_{x_j \in X} f_k(x_j, c_{t})}}\right]LN​=−EX​[log∑xj​∈X​fk​(xj​,ct​)fk​(xt+k​,ct​)​]

Eq. 4 in van den Oord, Li and Vinyals, "Representation learning with contrastive predictive coding", arXiv 1807.03748v2, Sec. 2.3.

  • X={x1,…,xN}X = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\}X={x1​,…,xN​}: the lineup. One sample is the true future piece; the other N−1N-1N−1 are negatives.
  • fk(xt+k,ct)\htmlClass{t-yellow}{f_k(x_{t+k}, c_t)}fk​(xt+k​,ct​): the score of the partner. CPC uses fk=exp⁡(zt+kTWkct)f_k = \exp(z_{t+k}^T W_k c_t)fk​=exp(zt+kT​Wk​ct​) (its Eq. 3), where zt+kz_{t+k}zt+k​ is the encoded piece and WkW_kWk​ is a learned matrix, one per step kkk.
  • ∑xj∈Xfk(xj,ct)\sum_{x_j \in X} f_k(x_j, c_t)∑xj​∈X​fk​(xj​,ct​): the scores of all NNN candidates, the partner included. Dividing by it is the softmax.
  • LN\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathcal{L}_{\text{N}}}LN​: minus the log of the partner's probability, averaged over lineups. The paper calls it "the categorical cross-entropy of classifying the positive sample correctly".

Where this came from

  • Gutmann and Hyvarinen (NCE, AISTATS 2010) learned a model by telling real data from noise, a yes-or-no question that InfoNCE turns into a multiple choice.
  • Wu et al. (1805.01978) treated every image as its own class, with a temperature and a memory bank of all 1.28M ImageNet embeddings (chapter 4).
  • CPC (1807.03748) named InfoNCE and its bound.
  • CPC v2 (1905.09272) rebuilt CPC for images and reached 71.5% top-1 (linear probe, ResNet-161, 200 epochs).
  • CMC (1906.05849) made the views different channels of one image, such as lightness and color.
  • Poole et al. (1905.06922) proved the InfoNCE bound exactly, beside other bounds on mutual information.

Where we go next: more candidates

The bound and the figure point the same way: a lineup with more strangers is a harder test, and its ceiling log⁡N\log NlogN is higher. But a batch only holds so many images. Chapter 4 shows two ways to get tens of thousands of negatives without a huge batch: a memory bank, then a momentum queue.

You should now be able to explain

  • Why InfoNCE is softmax cross-entropy where the classes are the candidates in the lineup.
  • What the temperature does to the softmax, and why cosine similarity needs one.
  • Why the mutual-information bound log⁡N−L\log N - \mathcal{L}logN−L can never exceed log⁡N\log NlogN.
  • Why a tighter bound is not the same as better features.

In practice

Track log⁡N\log NlogN next to your InfoNCE loss. A loss stuck at log⁡N\log NlogN means the model is guessing. A loss near 0 means the lineups are too easy to teach anything, so add negatives or make the views harder. Treat the temperature as a hyperparameter to tune, not a constant to copy, and do not read the mutual-information bound as a measure of feature quality.

Act IIThe recipes

Negatives at scale: a memory bank, then a momentum queue

The lineup from chapter 3 teaches more when it holds more strangers. So where do you find tens of thousands of negatives for every query, when a GPU holds only a few hundred images at once?

This chapter follows two answers. The first stores old embeddings and finds that they go stale. The second, MoCo, keeps a queue of recent ones and makes them from a slowly moving copy of the encoder.

The problem: a lineup needs many strangers

Recall the game. The network encodes one view of an image; call that vector the query. It also encodes a second view of the same image; call that the positive key. Then a softmax must pick the positive key out of a row of negative keys, the embeddings of other images. The query is chapter 3's anchor. The keys are its candidates: one positive key and many negative keys.

Why want many negatives? With five strangers in the lineup, they are probably all easy to tell apart from your partner. With fifty thousand, a few will look a lot like it: another mug, the same table. To pick the right one anyway, the encoder has to notice finer details. A harder lineup trains better features.

The obvious source of negatives is the rest of the batch: the other images you just encoded. The MoCo paper calls this end-to-end, because the gradient flows through every key. But then the number of negatives is tied to the batch size, and the batch is tied to GPU memory. On the authors' GPUs, the largest batch that fit was 1024 images. The MoCo v2 authors estimate that a batch of 4096 would need 93.0G of memory per GPU.

First fix: a memory bank

Wu et al. (2018) asked a different question: why compute negatives at all? Keep one stored embedding for every image in the dataset, in a table they call the memory bank. For ImageNet that is 1.28M vectors of 128 numbers, about 600 MB. Each step, draw negatives from the table instead of encoding them; Wu drew 4,096 per image. (Wu's paper calls this count mmm; it is unrelated to the momentum mmm below.)

The catch is in how the table is filled. An image's entry is rewritten only when that image comes round in training again, once per epoch. At a batch of 256, an epoch is about 5000 steps. So the negatives in one lineup were made by up to that many different versions of the encoder, some fresh and some an epoch old.

Picture trying to recognise a friend from today's photo by comparing it with a gallery of portraits. Each portrait was painted by the same artist, but years apart, and the artist's style kept changing. Two portraits that look different may differ only in when they were painted. Stale keys are like that: their differences mix up "different image" with "different encoder". The MoCo authors call such keys inconsistent.

MoCo's fix: a queue of recent keys from a slow copy

MoCo (Momentum Contrast) keeps two ideas apart. A queue holds the keys of the last few batches: each step, the new batch's keys go in at one end and the oldest batch falls out at the other. The queue length KKK no longer depends on the batch size. Because every key is at most a few hundred steps old, it is far fresher than a bank entry.

The second idea decides which network makes the keys. You cannot send gradients into the keys in the queue: the computation that made them finished many steps ago. So the keys come from a separate key encoder that gets no gradient at all. It is a slowly moving copy of the trained query encoder. Each step it moves a small fraction of the way toward the query encoder's current weights. The fraction is 1−m1 - m1−m, where mmm is the momentum (not the margin mmm of chapter 1).

The figure below makes this concrete in a toy. Imagine an encoder's millions of weights squeezed onto a plane. The query encoder (red ring: it is trained) jumps around with each noisy gradient step. The key encoder chases it. Every brown dot is the key encoder as it was when one batch now in the queue was encoded. The queue holds 16 batches, as a 4096-key queue does at batch 256.

Make a guess before you press "0". With m=0m = 0m=0, the key encoder becomes an exact copy of the query encoder at every step. The keys are then as fresh as they can be. Will training work better or worse?

Press it. The brown dots scatter as widely as the query encoder's own jumps, because each batch in the queue was encoded by a different network. The paper reports that at m=0m = 0m=0 "the training loss oscillates and fails to converge". Fresh is not enough: the keys must also agree with each other.

Now step through the chips. At m=0.9m = 0.9m=0.9 the cloud shrinks, and the sourced accuracy is 55.2. At 0.990.990.99 and 0.9990.9990.999 the queue's keys come from almost the same network, and accuracy peaks at 59.0. At 0.99990.99990.9999 the cloud is even tighter, but the key encoder now trails far behind the query encoder, and accuracy dips slightly, to 58.9. The paper does not test why; the lag in the toy is one possible reason (our reading).

The same idea as an equation: the loss

The loss is the lineup from chapter 3. Only the source of the strangers changes: they are the keys in the queue.

Lq=−log⁡exp⁡(q⋅k+/τ)∑i=0Kexp⁡(q⋅ki/τ)\htmlData{step=1, link=query}{\mathcal{L}_q} = -\log \frac{\exp(\htmlData{step=2, link=pos}{\htmlClass{t-blue}{q}{\cdot}\htmlClass{t-yellow}{k_+}} / \tau)}{\htmlData{step=3, link=queue}{\sum_{i=0}^{K}\exp(\htmlClass{t-blue}{q}{\cdot}\htmlClass{t-red}{k_i} / \tau)}}Lq​=−log∑i=0K​exp(q⋅ki​/τ)exp(q⋅k+​/τ)​

Eq. 1 in He et al., "Momentum contrast for unsupervised visual representation learning", arXiv 1911.05722v3.

  • q\htmlClass{t-blue}{q}q: the query, the query encoder's output for one view. A 128-number vector scaled to length 1.
  • k+\htmlClass{t-yellow}{k_+}k+​: the positive key, the key encoder's output for the other view of the same image.
  • ki\htmlClass{t-red}{k_i}ki​, i=0…Ki = 0 \dots Ki=0…K: the K+1K + 1K+1 candidates, the positive key plus KKK negatives from the queue. In the first MoCo the negatives are the queue only, never the other images of the current batch.
  • q⋅kq \cdot kq⋅k: the dot product, which is the cosine similarity because both vectors have length 1.
  • τ\tauτ: the temperature, which sharpens the softmax. MoCo uses τ=\tau =τ= 0.07.
  • Lq\mathcal{L}_qLq​: the cross-entropy of a (K+1)(K+1)(K+1)-way softmax whose correct answer is the positive key.

Try it with numbers, at τ=0.07\tau = 0.07τ=0.07 and three negatives. Say q⋅k+=0.8q \cdot k_+ = 0.8q⋅k+​=0.8. Divide every term by the positive's term, so each negative contributes exp⁡((q⋅ki−0.8)/0.07)\exp((q \cdot k_i - 0.8)/0.07)exp((q⋅ki​−0.8)/0.07).

  • Easy negatives at 0.30.30.3, 0.10.10.1 and −0.2-0.2−0.2 contribute e−7.1≈0.0008e^{-7.1} \approx 0.0008e−7.1≈0.0008 and less. The loss is log⁡(1+0.0008+… )≈0.0008\log(1 + 0.0008 + \dots) \approx 0.0008log(1+0.0008+…)≈0.0008: almost nothing to learn.
  • Swap the last one for a look-alike at 0.750.750.75. It contributes e−0.05/0.07=e−0.71≈0.49e^{-0.05/0.07} = e^{-0.71} \approx 0.49e−0.05/0.07=e−0.71≈0.49, and the loss jumps to log⁡(1.49)≈0.40\log(1.49) \approx 0.40log(1.49)≈0.40.

One look-alike carries almost the whole loss. With a small temperature, only near-misses teach. That is why a big lineup helps: the more strangers you draw, the more likely one of them is a near-miss.

The momentum update, and why it keeps keys consistent

Here is the rule that moves the key encoder. Read it as "keep most of where you are, and take a small step toward the query encoder".

θk←mθk+(1−m)θq.\htmlData{step=1, link=key}{\htmlClass{t-brown}{\theta_\textrm{k}}} \leftarrow \htmlData{step=2, link=momentum}{m \htmlClass{t-brown}{\theta_\textrm{k}}} + \htmlData{step=3, link=query}{(1 - m) \htmlClass{t-blue}{\theta_\textrm{q}}}.θk​←mθk​+(1−m)θq​.

Eq. 2 in He et al., arXiv 1911.05722v3.

  • θk\htmlClass{t-brown}{\theta_\textrm{k}}θk​: all the weights of the key encoder. No gradient ever reaches them.
  • θq\htmlClass{t-blue}{\theta_\textrm{q}}θq​: all the weights of the query encoder. "Only the parameters θq\theta_\textrm{q}θq​ are updated by back-propagation."
  • mmm: the momentum, between 0 and 1. MoCo's default is 0.999.

Try it with one weight. Say the query encoder's weight is 1.01.01.0 and the key encoder's is 000, with m=0.999m = 0.999m=0.999.

  • After one step, the key weight is 0.999⋅0+0.001⋅1.0=0.0010.999 \cdot 0 + 0.001 \cdot 1.0 = 0.0010.999⋅0+0.001⋅1.0=0.001. It closed 0.1%0.1\%0.1% of the gap.
  • If the query weight stayed put, the remaining gap would shrink by a factor 0.9990.9990.999 per step. It halves after ln⁡2/0.001≈\ln 2 / 0.001 \approxln2/0.001≈ 693 steps.
  • The oldest key in a queue of K=K =K= 65536 is 65536/256=65536 / 256 =65536/256= 256 steps old. Over those steps the key encoder closes at most 23% of its gap. The queue's keys were made by nearly the same network.
  • Compare the memory bank: an entry can be 5000 steps old. By then a key encoder with m=0.999m = 0.999m=0.999 would have only 0.7% of its gap left: a different network.

You might expect an encoder that moves a thousand times slower to learn a thousand times slower. It does not, because it follows the query encoder with a delay, not at a reduced speed. Each gradient step is noisy and jumps around. The key encoder averages roughly the last thousand of those jumps, so the noise cancels and the steady progress remains. Press "Run 500 steps" at m=0.999m = 0.999m=0.999: the key encoder glides along behind the query encoder's trail while the query encoder jitters.

Does it pay off?

The MoCo paper trained the same ResNet-50 three ways and changed only where the negatives come from. The chart below plots the results against the number of negatives KKK.

Three things to read off. Every curve rises with KKK: more strangers, better features. End-to-end and MoCo agree where both exist, so the queue costs nothing in quality at small KKK. And the memory bank sits below MoCo all the way, by 2.6 points at the largest KKK. That gap is the price of stale keys.

Check yourself: why can't MoCo just backpropagate into the key encoder, like it does into the query encoder?

The loss depends on every key in the queue, so a true gradient for the key encoder would have to flow into all of them. But most of those keys were computed in earlier steps, and their computation is gone. You could only backpropagate into the current batch's keys, which would make the key encoder a second trained network, changing fast, and the queue inconsistent again. MoCo instead gives the key encoder no gradient and moves it with Eq. 2.

Check yourself: what would m=1m = 1m=1 do?

The key encoder would never move from its starting weights. Its keys would be perfectly consistent, but they would come from a random network forever, and the query encoder would learn to match a random network's outputs. This is our reasoning; the paper's ablation stops at 0.9999.

Inside MoCo: forward, then backward

Here is one full training step with the paper's ImageNet setup. Make a guess before you press "6 Gradients": which boxes will the gradient reach?

The answer to the guess: only the query encoder (and the queries and logits on the way). Everything brown is updated without gradients: the key encoder by Eq. 2, the queue by enqueue and dequeue.

Why shuffle batch norm?

Batch normalization (BN) rescales each feature using statistics of the samples on the same GPU. Without care, a query and its positive key are normalized with statistics from the same group of samples. That shared statistic is a "signature" the network can use to find its partner without looking at the content. Without the fix, the accuracy on the training game (picking the partner) climbs above 99.9% while the features get worse. MoCo shuffles the batch order before it splits the key batch across GPUs, and shuffles back after. Query and positive key then see different statistics.

Where this came from

Wu, Xiong, Yu and Lin (1805.01978, 2018) introduced instance discrimination: treat every image as its own class, and keep the memory bank so the softmax over all images is affordable. Their ResNet-50 reached 54.0 top-1 on ImageNet, measured with a different linear classifier on an earlier layer.

He, Fan, Wu, Xie and Girshick (1911.05722, 2019) replaced the bank with the queue and the momentum encoder. MoCo's ResNet-50 reached 60.6 linear-probe top-1 after 200 epochs. (A linear probe, as in chapter 3, trains one classifier layer on frozen features.) Because the two papers measured differently, the two numbers are not a controlled comparison; the chart above is.

What changed next: MoCo v2 and v3

MoCo v2 (2003.04297) kept the queue and the small batch, and took two things from SimCLR: a two-layer MLP head (a projection head, explained in chapter 5) and blur augmentation. It also added a cosine learning-rate schedule and raised the temperature. The table below lists what each change bought.

MoCo v3 (2104.02057) moved to Vision Transformers (ViT) and teaches two lessons.

The first: with a big enough batch, the queue is unnecessary, but the momentum encoder still helps. With a batch of 4096, the batch already holds enough negatives, so v3 drops the queue: each query's negatives are the other images' keys in the batch. You might expect m=0m = 0m=0 to fail, as it did in v1. It does not, because all keys now come from the current network and are consistent anyway (our reading; the paper notes that m=0m = 0m=0 is then close to SimCLR). Yet a momentum encoder with m=m =m= 0.99 still adds 2.2 points. v3 also adds a prediction head on the query side, as BYOL does (chapter 8).

The second: training ViTs this way is quietly unstable. It does not diverge; it loses a few points, and you may not notice. Gradient spikes appeared first in the patch projection, the ViT's first layer, which turns image patches into vectors. The fix is to freeze that layer at its random initialization, so it never changes.

Where we go next: no queue, just a huge batch

MoCo got many negatives cheaply by keeping old keys. SimCLR (chapter 5) took the opposite route: no queue and no momentum encoder, just a batch of thousands, with everything trained end to end. It also found which augmentations matter, and why a throwaway head helps.

You should now be able to explain

  • Why more negatives help, and why the batch alone cannot supply them.
  • Why memory-bank keys are inconsistent, and how a queue plus a momentum encoder fixes that.
  • What Eq. 2 does with m=0.999m = 0.999m=0.999: a 0.1%0.1\%0.1% step per update, about 693 steps to close half a gap.
  • Which parts of MoCo get gradients, and which change by momentum or enqueueing instead.

In practice

If your GPU memory limits the batch, a momentum queue gives you many negatives cheaply. In the MoCo v2 measurements, MoCo at batch 256 used 5.0G per GPU against 7.4G for end-to-end. With very large batches, as in MoCo v3, the queue adds little, but a momentum encoder still helps. Treat mmm as a delay in steps, about 1/(1−m)1/(1-m)1/(1−m), so about 1000 steps at m=0.999m = 0.999m=0.999, as in the worked example above: a short training run needs a smaller mmm (our reading).

SimCLR: strong augmentation, a big batch, a throwaway head

MoCo built a queue and a momentum encoder to get many negatives. SimCLR asks whether you need any of that. Its answer is no, if you get three plain choices right. The most important choice is how you make the two views.

Make a guess before you press "2nd: Color". The figure starts with crop alone. Which do you think trains better features: crop alone, or crop followed by color distortion? And what could the network learn from crops alone that would not help it later?

Lesson 1: crop alone lets the network cheat

Look at the histograms under the two views when only crop is on. Two crops of one photo share almost the same colors: the same beige wall, the same wooden table, the same mug. A crop of a different photo has different colors. So the network can find the partner by comparing color statistics alone, without ever learning what a mug looks like. That is a shortcut: a cheap feature that solves the training game and is useless afterwards.

Now press "2nd: Color". The partner's colors shift, and the green overlap shrinks. Color can no longer identify the partner, so the network must use what color distortion leaves alone: edges, shapes, the layout of the scene. The table shows the effect: crop alone gives 33.1, crop then color gives 56.3, and color then crop gives 55.8. The paper makes the same argument: color histograms alone suffice to tell its crops apart, so it composes cropping with color distortion.

You might expect each transformation to be good on its own. In fact the diagonal is weak everywhere: color alone gives 18.8 and blur alone 2.6. A good task needs views that differ in many ways at once, so that only the content of the photo connects them.

The right strength is also not the one supervised learning likes. The paper varies the strength of color distortion:

SimCLR Table 1: ImageNet top-1 with ResNet-50. SimCLR rows are linear probes after 100 epochs of pretraining; supervised rows are ResNet-50s trained for 90 epochs with the same augmentation. The two rows use different protocols; compare the trends, not the levels.
Color distortion strength1/81/41/211 (+Blur)AutoAugment (a learned augmentation policy)
SimCLR (linear probe, 100 epochs)59.661.062.663.264.561.1
Supervised (90 epochs)77.076.776.575.775.477.1

Stronger color distortion helps SimCLR and slightly hurts the supervised model. With labels, color distortion is just noise. Without labels, the augmentation is the task: it decides what the network must learn to ignore.

Check yourself: you train with crop only on product photos where every product has its own color. The training loss drops fast. Why might the features still be poor?

The loss can be solved by color matching: each product's crops share a color, and other products' crops do not. The encoder learns color statistics, not shapes, so a classifier on top of it has little to work with. Add color distortion (and grey-scale views) so that color no longer identifies the partner.

Lesson 2: the other views in the batch are the negatives

Now the loss. Take a batch of NNN photos and make two views of each, so you have 2N2N2N views. Pick one view as the anchor. Its partner is the positive. Every one of the other 2(N−1)2(N-1)2(N−1) views comes from a different photo, so each of them is a negative. There is no memory bank and no queue: the batch is the lineup.

Careful: NNN now counts photos, not candidates. Each row's lineup has 2N−12N - 12N−1 candidates.

Why does this work without MoCo's tricks? Every negative is computed in this step, by the encoder as it is now. A memory bank holds embeddings from earlier versions of the encoder, so they are stale; MoCo's momentum encoder keeps its queue consistent by changing slowly. In-batch negatives are never stale, so neither fix is needed. The price is the batch size: to see many negatives, you need a large batch, and that is the second ingredient.

The figure below draws the whole loss for a tiny batch. On the left, the views sit on the unit circle (each embedding scaled to length 1). On the right is the table of cosine similarities between every pair of views, with views 2k−12k-12k−1 and 2k2k2k from photo kkk, as in the paper.

You might expect the diagonal to be the positive, as in a table of images against captions. Here it is not: the diagonal compares a view with itself, so its cosine is always 1 and it teaches nothing. The loss removes it. The positive sits next to the diagonal, at the partner's column.

The same idea as an equation

Read one row of the table as one softmax: "of all the other views, which is my partner?". SimCLR calls this loss NT-Xent, the normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy.

ℓi,j=−log⁡exp⁡(sim(zi,zj)/τ)∑k=12N1[k≠i]exp⁡(sim(zi,zk)/τ)\ell_{i,j} = -\log \frac{\htmlData{step=1, link=pos}{\htmlClass{t-yellow}{\exp(\htmlData{step=2, link=sim}{\mathrm{sim}(\bm z_i, \bm z_j)}/\htmlData{step=4, link=tau}{\tau})}}}{\htmlData{step=3, link=row}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\sum_{k=1}^{2N}}} \htmlData{step=5, link=mask}{\mathbb{1}_{[k \neq i]}}\htmlClass{t-red}{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(\bm z_i, \bm z_k)/\tau)}}ℓi,j​=−log∑k=12N​1[k=i]​exp(sim(zi​,zk​)/τ)exp(sim(zi​,zj​)/τ)​

Eq. 1 in Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi and Hinton, "A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations", arXiv 2002.05709v3 (the indicator is written there with a blackboard-bold 1, macro \one).

  • zi,zj\bm z_i, \bm z_jzi​,zj​: the head's outputs for two views of the same photo. iii is the anchor's row; jjj is the partner's column.
  • sim(u,v)=u⊤v/(∥u∥∥v∥)\mathrm{sim}(\bm u, \bm v) = \bm u^\top \bm v / (\lVert \bm u\rVert \lVert \bm v\rVert)sim(u,v)=u⊤v/(∥u∥∥v∥): the cosine similarity, one cell of the table. Dividing by the lengths is the "normalized" in NT-Xent.
  • τ\tauτ: the temperature. Dividing by a small τ\tauτ stretches the gaps between cosines before the softmax.
  • ∑k=12N\htmlClass{t-red}{\sum_{k=1}^{2N}}∑k=12N​: a sum over the whole row, all 2N2N2N views.
  • 1[k≠i]\mathbb{1}_{[k \neq i]}1[k=i]​: 1 for every column except k=ik = ik=i, so the diagonal cell drops out. The row keeps the partner and the 2(N−1)2(N-1)2(N−1) negatives.

Try it with the numbers in the figure: N=2N = 2N=2 and τ=0.5\tau = 0.5τ=0.5 (our choice for the arithmetic; the paper does not give a default). Row 1 has cosines 0.8 with its partner, 0 and -0.6 with the two negatives.

  • Divide by τ\tauτ: 1.6, 0, −1.21.6,\ 0,\ -1.21.6, 0, −1.2.
  • Exponentiate: e1.6≈4.95, e0=1, e−1.2≈0.30e^{1.6} \approx 4.95,\ e^{0} = 1,\ e^{-1.2} \approx 0.30e1.6≈4.95, e0=1, e−1.2≈0.30. The row sum is 6.256.256.25.
  • The partner's probability is 4.95/6.25≈0.794.95 / 6.25 \approx 0.794.95/6.25≈0.79, so ℓ1,2=−log⁡0.79≈0.23\ell_{1,2} = -\log 0.79 \approx 0.23ℓ1,2​=−log0.79≈0.23.

Each row is one loss. The batch loss averages all of them, both directions of every pair:

L=12N∑k=1N[ℓ(2k ⁣− ⁣1,2k)+ℓ(2k,2k ⁣− ⁣1)]\mathcal{L} = \htmlData{step=1, link=rows}{\frac{1}{2N} \sum_{k=1}^N} \left[ \htmlData{step=2, link=pos}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\ell(2k\!-\!1, 2k)}} + \htmlData{step=3, link=pos}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\ell(2k, 2k\!-\!1)}}\right]L=2N1​k=1∑N​[ℓ(2k−1,2k)+ℓ(2k,2k−1)]

Algorithm 1 in Chen et al., arXiv 2002.05709v3 (unnumbered there).

For our tiny batch at τ=0.5\tau = 0.5τ=0.5, the four row losses average to the "mean over all rows" printed under the table. Now press N = 4. Every row goes from 2 negatives to 6, and the anchor's loss rises, because there are more strangers who might look like the partner. At N=4096N = 4096N=4096, SimCLR's default batch, each row has 8190 negatives (our arithmetic, 2(N−1)2(N-1)2(N−1)). The paper itself gives 16382 negatives per positive pair at batch 8192.

What about τ\tauτ? The paper does not state one default. In its sweep (Table 5, 100 epochs, with the embeddings normalized), τ=0.1\tau = 0.1τ=0.1 gave the best linear-probe top-1, 64.4, against 59.7 at 0.05 and 58.0 at 1. Why a small temperature helps, and why too small hurts, is the subject of chapter 6.

Lesson 3: a head you train and then throw away

From here on, the embedding is what the loss sees (z\bm zz), and the representation is the encoder output you keep (h\bm hh). Before this chapter there was no head, so the two were the same vector.

The loss wants the two views to land on the same point. To do that, the network must remove everything the augmentation changed: the color shift, the crop position, the blur. That is what we asked for, but it removes too much. Color can matter for the next task: a ripe banana and a green one differ only in color.

SimCLR's fix is a small extra network, the projection head ggg, between the encoder and the loss. The encoder produces h\bm hh; the head turns it into z=g(h)\bm z = g(\bm h)z=g(h); the loss sees only z\bm zz. Now the head can do the forgetting. It learns to throw away color and orientation, so z\bm zz is invariant, while h\bm hh, one layer earlier, is free to keep them. After pretraining you delete ggg and keep h\bm hh.

Think of h\bm hh as your full notes and ggg as a cheat sheet written for one exam. The exam only asks "same photo or not?", so the cheat sheet leaves out the colors. For the next exam, you bring the notes.

The paper measures both halves of this story. A nonlinear head (one hidden layer with a ReLU) beats a linear head by 3 points, and beats no head by more than 10 points. Even with the nonlinear head, h\bm hh beats z\bm zz by more than 10 points under a linear probe (Sec. 4.2; the bars in its Fig. 8 carry no printed values). To test the "forgetting" idea, the authors train a small classifier to guess which transformation was applied, from h\bm hh or from g(h)g(\bm h)g(h):

SimCLR Table 3: accuracy of predicting the transformation applied during pretraining, from h or from g(h). For this test both are 2048 numbers wide. The last column is the score of always guessing the most common answer: grey-scale is applied with probability 0.2, so always guessing "color" is right 80% of the time.
What to predictfrom hfrom g(h)always guess the common answer
color or grey-scale99.397.480
rotation (4 angles)67.625.625
original or corrupted99.559.650
original or Sobel-filtered96.656.350

From g(h)g(\bm h)g(h), rotation is at chance level: the head has thrown it away. From h\bm hh it is still there. The paper offers this as its conjecture for why the head helps, and the table supports it.

Check yourself: the loss is computed on z, so z is what training optimized. Why is it the worse representation?

Because the loss rewards invariance to the augmentations, and z is where that invariance is enforced. Anything the augmentations change, such as color or orientation, is information z is pushed to discard. The layer before the head is only asked to make that job possible, so it can keep more of the photo. A downstream task that needs color or orientation finds them in h, not in z.

Inside SimCLR: forward, then backward

Here is one training step of the real model, as a slide per stage. Step through it with Next. The line under the drawing gives each tensor's shape, computed from the paper's configuration; the batch buttons change NNN and recompute them. Before you reach the backward stages, guess: which boxes will the gradient reach?

Bigger batches and longer training

More negatives per step make the lineup harder, and a harder lineup teaches more. The paper's Table B.1 measures this directly: ResNet-50, linear probe, learning rate scaled linearly with the batch.

SimCLR Table B.1 (left of each slash in the paper: linear learning-rate scaling): ImageNet linear-probe top-1 (%) of ResNet-50 by batch size and pretraining epochs. The paper also reports square-root scaling, which helps small batches at few epochs.
Batch size100 epochs200400800
25657.561.964.766.6
51260.764.066.267.8
102462.865.367.268.5
204864.066.168.168.9
409664.666.568.268.9
819264.866.667.869.0

Read it by rows and by columns. At 100 epochs, going from batch 256 to 8192 gains more than seven points. At 800 epochs the same change gains less than three, because training longer also shows the model more negatives over time. The paper frames this as contrastive learning benefiting more than supervised learning from big batches and long training, and explains it by the negatives. Its supervised check covers only the length of training (a supervised ResNet does not improve when trained longer, App. B.3); it has no supervised batch-size sweep.

Where this came from

SimCLR is by Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi and Hinton (2002.05709, submitted 2020-02-13). In-batch negatives were not new; the N-pair loss in chapter 1 already used them. The contribution was a careful ablation that found which simple parts matter, with no special architecture and no memory bank. Its ResNet-50 reaches 69.3 top-1 on ImageNet under a linear probe after 1000 epochs of pretraining, and a four-times-wider ResNet-50 reaches 76.5 under the same protocol.

What came next

InfoMin (Tian et al., 2005.10243) explains Lesson 1: good views share only the information the downstream task needs, so you reduce what the two views have in common but keep what matters for the label. Too little shared information makes the task impossible; too much lets shortcuts like color matching in.

SimCLRv2 (2006.10029) scaled the same recipe to bigger networks and used it to learn from a small fraction of labels. MoCo v2 borrowed SimCLR's MLP head and blur and kept its queue, so it needs no huge batch (chapter 4).

Where we go next

You now have a full recipe. But why should "pull the pair, push the rest" produce good features at all, and what does the temperature really control? Chapter 6 answers this on the sphere. First, the interlude runs one complete SimCLR step at full size.

You should now be able to explain

  • Why crop alone lets the network match color histograms, and why adding color distortion removes that shortcut.
  • How the other 2(N−1)2(N-1)2(N−1) views in a batch serve as negatives, why they are never stale, and what the masked diagonal is.
  • Why a projection head used only for the loss leaves the layer before it more useful, and why it is thrown away.
  • Why SimCLR needs a large batch, and what that costs.

In practice

Start from the augmentations, not the loss. Ask what your downstream task must ignore and what it must keep: if color matters (ripe or unripe, rust or paint), weaken color distortion or keep a head and use the features before it. Always evaluate the encoder output h\bm hh, not the head output. If you cannot afford a batch of thousands, use a queue (chapter 4) instead of shrinking the lineup. With data-parallel training, make sure batch normalization statistics are shared across devices, or the model may cheat.

Interlude

One SimCLR training step, end to end

When the loss goes down, what does each negative actually do to the anchor? Chapter 5 walked SimCLR's step box by box; this interlude runs the same step on drawn photos and stops where that question is answered, at the gradient.

Click a stage or press Next. The stages before the gradient are a quick recap; the shapes and settings are explained in chapter 5, and the equations in chapter 3 and chapter 5. New batch draws four other photos and new random views.

Then the next batch arrives and the step repeats, for 100 epochs in the paper's ablations and 1000 for its best models. When training ends, the head is deleted and the ResNet-50's h\bm hh is what you keep.

Check yourself: in one row at N = 4096, how many cells get a push, and which one gets a pull?

The row has 8192 cells. The diagonal (the anchor against itself) is masked and gets nothing. The partner view, the other view of the same photo, gets the pull. The remaining 8190 cells are negatives, and each gets a push weighted by its softmax probability divided by the temperature, so most of the push comes from the few negatives that look most like the anchor.

You should now be able to explain

  • Which cells of a row push the anchor, which one pulls it, and why close negatives push hardest.
  • Where the negatives come from, how many each row has, and why the diagonal is removed.
  • Which weights the gradient reaches, and what is thrown away after training.

In practice

The cosine table grows with the square of the batch, so in common multi-device implementations it is split. (This is our note; the paper does not describe it.) Each device computes the rows for its own views against all views gathered from every device. If you reimplement this, gather the embeddings across devices before the matrix product, or each row will see only its own device's negatives. Pool batch-norm statistics across devices too.

Act IIIWhy it works

Alignment and uniformity on the sphere

You now know how to train with InfoNCE, but what does it actually do to the embeddings? This chapter shows that it does two jobs at once, pulling partners together and spreading everything out, and that the temperature decides how the two trade off.

The picture: points on a ball

Almost every method on this page divides each embedding by its length before it compares two of them. Every embedding then has length 1, so it is a point on the surface of a ball: a sphere. In three dimensions you can see it; real models use many more dimensions, but the picture is the same. On the sphere the dot product of two embeddings is their cosine similarity, a number between -1 and 1, and only directions matter.

Why normalize at all? Without it, the encoder could make the softmax confident by just making vectors longer, without learning anything new. With unit length, the only way to raise a score is to point in a better direction. The temperature τ\tauτ then sets the scale that the softmax sees.

The figure trains a small encoder that maps 90 made-up images onto the sphere. Each image has two views: a blue dot (view A) and a yellow dot (view B), joined by a green line. The images come from six hidden classes that the loss never sees; the 15 images of one class are drawn as big dots, so you can follow them.

Make a guess before you press "Alignment only". This loss only asks the two views of each image to land close together. Where will the 90 images end up?

Press it. Everything slides to a single spot on the sphere. You have seen this in chapter 1: if every image gets the same embedding, every pair agrees perfectly and the loss is zero. It is collapse again, now on a sphere.

Now press "InfoNCE". The same pull is still there, but the negatives in the denominator push every image away from every other one. The dots spread over the whole sphere, and each green line stays short.

Two forces: alignment and uniformity

Wang and Isola gave these two effects names. Alignment means the two views of an image land close together. Uniformity means all embeddings together cover the sphere evenly, with no crowded spots and no empty ones.

Think of people arriving in an empty waiting room. Strangers sit as far from each other as they can, so the room fills evenly: that is uniformity. Couples still sit side by side: that is alignment. Nobody wants a crowd, and no couple wants to be split up.

Why is an even spread good? Points that are spread out can be told apart. If many different images crowd into one region, their embeddings are nearly the same, and whatever made them different is lost. An even spread uses all the room the sphere has, so it keeps the most information about the images.

The two forces as equations

Both forces can be measured with a short formula. Alignment is the average distance between the two views of an image:

Lalign(f;α)≜E(x,y)∼ppos[∥f(x)−f(y)∥2α],α>0.\mathcal{L}_\mathsf{align}(f; \alpha) \triangleq \htmlData{step=2, link=align}{\mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim p_\mathsf{pos}}} \left[ \htmlData{step=1, link=align}{\htmlClass{t-green}{\|f(x) - f(y)\|_2^\alpha}} \right], \quad \alpha > 0.Lalign​(f;α)≜E(x,y)∼ppos​​[∥f(x)−f(y)∥2α​],α>0.

Unnumbered, Sec. 4.1.1 in Wang and Isola, "Understanding contrastive representation learning through alignment and uniformity on the hypersphere", ICML 2020, arXiv 2005.10242v10.

Uniformity looks at two images picked independently, not a pair. It scores how close they are with a bump that is 1 when they touch and falls toward 0 as they move apart, then averages over all such pairs:

Luniform(f;t)≜log⁡Ex,y∼i.i.d.pdata[e−t∥f(x)−f(y)∥22],t>0.\mathcal{L}_\mathsf{uniform}(f; t) \triangleq \htmlData{step=2}{\log \mathbb{E}_{x, y \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} p_\mathsf{data}}} \left[ \htmlData{step=1, link=uniform}{\htmlClass{t-red}{e^{-t \|f(x) - f(y)\|_2^2}}} \right], \quad t > 0.Luniform​(f;t)≜logEx,y∼i.i.d.pdata​​[e−t∥f(x)−f(y)∥22​],t>0.

Unnumbered, Sec. 4.1.2 in Wang and Isola, arXiv 2005.10242v10 (written there with a Gaussian potential Gt(u,v)=e−t∥u−v∥22G_t(u, v) = e^{-t\|u - v\|_2^2}Gt​(u,v)=e−t∥u−v∥22​).

  • ≜\triangleq≜ means "is defined as"; i.i.d. means drawn independently from the same distribution.
  • fff: the encoder; f(x)f(x)f(x) is a unit-length embedding.
  • (x,y)∼ppos(x, y) \sim p_\mathsf{pos}(x,y)∼ppos​: a positive pair, the two views of one image.
  • x,y∼i.i.d.pdatax, y \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} p_\mathsf{data}x,y∼i.i.d.pdata​: two images drawn independently from the data, usually two different images.
  • ∥f(x)−f(y)∥2α\htmlClass{t-green}{\|f(x) - f(y)\|_2^\alpha}∥f(x)−f(y)∥2α​: the distance between partners, raised to the power α\alphaα. The paper's code uses α=2\alpha = 2α=2.
  • e−t∥f(x)−f(y)∥22\htmlClass{t-red}{e^{-t\|f(x) - f(y)\|_2^2}}e−t∥f(x)−f(y)∥22​: the bump, the push between two images. The larger ttt, the faster it falls, so the more it only cares about near neighbours. The code uses t=2t = 2t=2.
  • log⁡E\log \mathbb{E}logE: the log of the average bump. Both losses are lower when better.

Try Luniform\mathcal L_\mathsf{uniform}Luniform​ with t=2t = 2t=2 on three points on a circle of radius 1. On the unit sphere, ∥u−v∥2=2−2 uTv\|u - v\|^2 = 2 - 2\,u^\mathsf{T} v∥u−v∥2=2−2uTv, so you only need the angles. Average over the three distinct pairs, as the paper's code does.

  • All three on one spot: every distance is 0, every bump is 1, and L=log⁡1=0\mathcal L = \log 1 = 0L=log1=0. This is the worst value, the collapsed sphere you just saw.
  • Two on one spot, the third opposite (squared distance 4): the bumps are 1, e−8e^{-8}e−8 and e−8e^{-8}e−8, so L=log⁡((1+2e−8)/3)≈−1.10\mathcal L = \log\big((1 + 2e^{-8})/3\big) \approx -1.10L=log((1+2e−8)/3)≈−1.10.
  • Evenly spaced, 120 degrees apart: each squared distance is 2−2cos⁡120∘=32 - 2\cos 120^\circ = 32−2cos120∘=3, each bump is e−6e^{-6}e−6, and L=−6\mathcal L = -6L=−6. The even spread wins by far.

Alignment is simpler: two pairs whose views are 0.2 and 0.4 apart give Lalign=(0.22+0.42)/2=0.10\mathcal L_\mathsf{align} = (0.2^2 + 0.4^2)/2 = 0.10Lalign​=(0.22+0.42)/2=0.10 with α=2\alpha = 2α=2.

The theorem: InfoNCE is these two forces

So far these are two nice measurements. The surprise is that InfoNCE optimizes exactly these two things. Wang and Isola take the loss with MMM negatives and let MMM grow without limit. The loss grows like log⁡M\log MlogM, so they subtract that, and what remains splits into two terms:

lim⁡M→∞Lcontrastive(f;τ,M)−log⁡M=−1τE(x,y)∼ppos[f(x)Tf(y)]+Ex∼pdata[log⁡Ex−∼pdata[ef(x−)Tf(x)/τ]]\htmlData{step=1, link=tau}{\lim_{M \rightarrow \infty} \mathcal{L}_\mathsf{contrastive}(f; \tau, M) - \log M} = \htmlData{step=2, link=align}{\htmlClass{t-green}{-\frac{1}{\tau} \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim p_\mathsf{pos}}\left[f(x)^{\mathsf{T}} f(y)\right]}} + \htmlData{step=3, link=uniform}{\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\mathsf{data}}\left[\log \mathbb{E}_{x^- \sim p_\mathsf{data}}\left[e^{f(x^-)^{\mathsf{T}} f(x) / \tau}\right]\right]}}M→∞lim​Lcontrastive​(f;τ,M)−logM=−τ1​E(x,y)∼ppos​​[f(x)Tf(y)]+Ex∼pdata​​[logEx−∼pdata​​[ef(x−)Tf(x)/τ]]

Eq. 2 (Theorem 1), Sec. 4.2 in Wang and Isola, arXiv 2005.10242v10; the proof is in App. A.2.

  • Lcontrastive(f;τ,M)\mathcal L_\mathsf{contrastive}(f; \tau, M)Lcontrastive​(f;τ,M): InfoNCE with one positive and MMM negatives (their Eq. 1, the loss of chapter 3).
  • −1τE[f(x)Tf(y)]\htmlClass{t-green}{-\tfrac{1}{\tau}\mathbb{E}[f(x)^\mathsf{T} f(y)]}−τ1​E[f(x)Tf(y)]: the alignment term. It is smallest when every pair of views lands on the same point.
  • Ex[log⁡Ex−[⋯ ]]\htmlClass{t-red}{\mathbb{E}_x[\log \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[\cdots]]}Ex​[logEx−​[⋯]]: the uniformity term. For each image it measures how crowded its neighbourhood is. The paper proves that a perfectly uniform encoder, if one exists, minimizes it.
  • Careful: MMM here is the number of negatives, the N−1N - 1N−1 of chapter 3.
  • The paper also shows that, with MMM negatives, the gap to this limit shrinks like M−1/2M^{-1/2}M−1/2. More negatives bring InfoNCE closer to this clean split.

Try the right side with numbers. Take τ=0.5\tau = 0.5τ=0.5 and partners at cosine 0.9: the alignment term is −0.9/0.5=−1.8-0.9/0.5 = -1.8−0.9/0.5=−1.8. If every negative sits at cosine 0, the uniformity term is log⁡e0=0\log e^{0} = 0loge0=0. Move half of the negatives to cosine 0.5 and it becomes log⁡((1+e1)/2)≈0.62\log\big((1 + e^{1})/2\big) \approx 0.62log((1+e1)/2)≈0.62: crowding raises the loss.

Why are these the same two forces? Use the identity from the worked example, uTv=1−12∥u−v∥2u^\mathsf{T} v = 1 - \tfrac12\|u - v\|^2uTv=1−21​∥u−v∥2 for unit vectors (derived here):

−1τ uTv=12τ∥u−v∥2−1τeuTv/τ=e1/τ e−12τ∥u−v∥2\htmlData{step=1, link=align}{\htmlClass{t-green}{-\tfrac{1}{\tau}\, u^\mathsf{T} v = \tfrac{1}{2\tau}\|u - v\|^2 - \tfrac{1}{\tau}}} \qquad \htmlData{step=2, link=uniform}{\htmlClass{t-red}{e^{u^\mathsf{T} v / \tau} = e^{1/\tau}\, e^{-\frac{1}{2\tau} \|u - v\|^2}}}−τ1​uTv=2τ1​∥u−v∥2−τ1​euTv/τ=e1/τe−2τ1​∥u−v∥2

Derived here from Eq. 2 of Wang and Isola, using unit-length embeddings.

The first term is Lalign\mathcal L_\mathsf{align}Lalign​ with α=2\alpha = 2α=2, scaled and shifted. The second is the same bump as in Luniform\mathcal L_\mathsf{uniform}Luniform​, with t=1/(2τ)t = 1/(2\tau)t=1/(2τ); the only difference is where the log sits, which the paper says does not change the best encoder. Take τ=0.5\tau = 0.5τ=0.5: then t=1t = 1t=1. Take τ=0.1\tau = 0.1τ=0.1: then t=5t = 5t=5, a much narrower bump. That one line already tells you what temperature does.

Check yourself: what would you get if you trained with Luniform\mathcal L_\mathsf{uniform}Luniform​ alone?

An even spread with no meaning. Nothing would ask the two views of an image to agree, so the encoder could scatter them anywhere, and the crop or the colors could decide where an image lands. When Wang and Isola fine-tune a trained encoder with only one of the two losses, its accuracy drops; with both, it rises (their Fig. 8). You need both forces.

Temperature: how local the push is

The bridge above says that a small τ\tauτ gives a narrow bump: an image only feels the neighbours right next to it, and it feels them strongly. A large τ\tauτ gives a wide bump: every image feels a gentle push from almost everyone. Chapter 7 shows the same thing from the gradient: each negative's share of the push grows like es/τe^{s/\tau}es/τ, where sss is its similarity to the anchor.

Now press the temperature buttons, then "InfoNCE", and watch the big dots. At τ=0.1\tau = 0.1τ=0.1 the sphere is covered most evenly, but the big dots, one hidden class, are spread far apart. At τ=1.0\tau = 1.0τ=1.0 they stay in a tight group, and the sphere is covered less evenly. The readout gives the numbers.

You might expect the most uniform sphere to be the best one. It is not, because of what sits next to an image. Its nearest neighbours are often images of the same kind: another mug, another dog. A small τ\tauτ pushes exactly those neighbours hardest, so it tears apart groups that you wanted to keep. Wang and Liu call this the uniformity-tolerance dilemma. Tolerance is the average similarity of two images from the same class. It needs labels, so it is only a check, never part of training.

In short, a lower τ\tauτ buys uniformity, and a higher one buys tolerance (Wang and Liu, Sec. 4.2). In the toy, most of the change happens between τ=0.5\tau = 0.5τ=0.5 and 1.01.01.0; below that the toy hardly changes. The toy has no accuracy to peak, so it cannot tell you the best τ\tauτ. For real networks the claim card below gives it.

Where this came from

Two papers built this view: Wang and Isola (ICML 2020) for the two forces, and Wang and Liu (CVPR 2021) for the temperature. Here is what each one claims, and how strong the evidence is.

Claim card: alignment and uniformity predict feature quality (Wang and Isola)

Claim
Encoders with lower Lalign\mathcal L_\mathsf{align}Lalign​ and Luniform\mathcal L_\mathsf{uniform}Luniform​ transfer better, and training on these two losses alone gives features as good as InfoNCE or better.
How
They trained many encoders per dataset (304 on STL-10, 45 on ImageNet-100), sweeping loss weights, τ\tauτ, α\alphaα and ttt, and report the best of each family with a linear probe (picked by 5-fold cross-validation; for STL-10 among the 150 encoders with 128-d output and batch 768).
Result
STL-10, small AlexNet-style encoder, linear probe on the output: InfoNCE 80.46%, align + uniform 81.15% (Table 1). ImageNet-100, ResNet-50 trained with MoCo for 240 epochs (an unofficial MoCo implementation), linear top-1: 72.80% vs 74.60% (Table 3). ImageNet-1K, ResNet-50 with MoCo v2 for 200 epochs, linear top-1: 67.5% from the official MoCo v2 code vs 67.69% (Table 5).
Caveat
On text (BookCorpus sentence embeddings, Table 4) the two losses alone are 3 to 4 points worse than InfoNCE, for example InfoNCE 77.51% vs align + uniform 73.76% on movie-review sentiment. The claim holds for the vision tables only.
Would fail if
Under a matched sweep, the align + uniform encoders lost consistently, as they do on text.

Claim card: temperature trades uniformity for tolerance (Wang and Liu)

Claim
A smaller τ\tauτ gives a more uniform but less tolerant embedding, and linear accuracy peaks in between.
How
ResNet-18 on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and SVHN, ResNet-50 on ImageNet100; negatives from a memory bank (a stored feature for every training image, see chapter 4), not from the batch; 200 epochs, batch 128; linear probe. They sweep τ\tauτ from 0.05 to 1.0. Their uniformity column prints −Luniform-\mathcal L_\mathsf{uniform}−Luniform​, so larger means more uniform there.
Result
CIFAR10 (Table 1) below: uniformity falls and tolerance rises as τ\tauτ grows. The best accuracy comes at τ\tauτ = 0.2 or 0.3 (Sec. 5.3).
